items.summary: Hashing Is Not Retrieval is a prospectively frozen three-arm evaluation of context accumulation in small-model multi-agent code cartography. It compares three ways for an orchestrator to hand work to a worker: 1. FULL HISTORY — retransmit prior worker outputs. 2. OPAQUE REF — replace the previous output with an unretrievable SHA-256 digest. 3. RETRIEVED — resolve the digest through a tenant-scoped content-addressed store and inject the recovered bytes. All arms receive identical source-derived evidence. The apparatus measures the exact message content sent to workers and records token counts, model and provider identifiers, generation IDs, usage, cost, retries, and retrieval proofs. A five-task gate preceded a fixed 50-task controlled benchmark, followed by a separate state-required evaluation across 24 deterministic fixtures and a five-scale Medusa case study. Key result: in the controlled benchmark, RETRIEVED reduced paired peak context by 38.3% relative to FULL HISTORY. The state-required follow-up shows that opaque references fail when state must be recovered, while verified retrieval preserves substantially more structural information. This is bounded-context evidence for automatic orchestrator-resolved state passing inside a specific two-worker code-cartography harness — not a universal claim about autonomous memory, long-context capability, or reasoning quality. The release includes the corrected author-identified preprint, executable apparatus, frozen results, task fixtures, telemetry, and verification instructions. Version 1.0.2 supplies the curated, verifier-passing reproducibility archive. It supersedes the uncurated archive from version 1.0.1 and includes the exact pinned apparatus, state-required fixtures, frozen results, and archive verifier. Submission status: This preprint was submitted to the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Long Context Foundation Models (LCFM). LCFM is a non-archival workshop; this Zenodo record is a public preprint and does not indicate acceptance or publication. Workshop information: https://longcontextfm.github.io/ Research website: https://abdulmoizahmed.com/research Concept DOI (all versions): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22844754 License: CC BY 4.0.

items.summary: State observation over the Hamilton division algebra is formulated as a structured realization problem for quaternionic multi-input multi-output systems. A left-intertwiner equation unifies companion assignment, row-oriented robust pole assignment, and coupled target realization with explicit noncommutative product order. A unitary measured-subspace decomposition yields a derivative-free observer with n-r dynamic quaternion states, where r = rank C, and reduces observability and detectability to a smaller pair. This order is minimal within the stated quaternion-linear full-state observer class. For full-order observers, structured H2 Lyapunov equations and an exact fixed-target gradient allow noise attenuation without moving the spectrum. For minimum-order observers, the reconstruction exposes the direct noise term and its interaction with pole-invariant injection freedom. Discrete-time formulas include the finite contribution of direct feedthrough, and correlated redundant outputs are characterized as noise references. Reproducible studies verify the gradients, compare quaternion, structured-complex, and real representations, expose the noise-cost nonuniqueness of maximum-volume designs, and test coupled repeated-class targets and a multi-output minimum-order observer.
items.title: Full- and Minimum-Order Quaternionic MIMO Observers: Spectral Assignment and Noise Geometry

items.summary: Handwritten archival tables contain rich historical information, yet transforming them into structured representations, such as Knowledge Graphs, requires integrating table structure recognition, handwriting recognition, and semantic interpretation - a complex multimodal process. End-to-end AI implementations can obscure these steps, resulting in opaque algorithmic operations that hinder human oversight, critical assessment, and trust. To address this, we present a modular, provenance-aware pipeline to convert handwritten tabular images into KGs supporting human-AI collaboration. The pipeline decomposes the workflow into three stages - table reconstruction, information extraction, and KG construction - while exposing intermediate representations for inspection, evaluation, and correction. A key contribution of our approach is the systematic integration of data provenance at every stage, ensuring that all extracted entities and literals remain traceable to their visual and textual origins. The proposed pipeline is demonstrated through a number of experiments on real-world archival material concerning military careers. The results across three different table reconstruction variants highlight the importance of modularisation. By coupling modularity with data provenance, our work advances transparent and collaboratively controllable image-to-KG pipelines for complex historical data.
items.title: From Historical Tabular Image to Knowledge Graphs: A Provenance-Aware Modular Pipeline

items.summary: # FaultNet This archive contains the trained models, example earthquake catalog, and Jupyter notebook used to apply **FaultNet**, a deep-learning framework for reconstructing three-dimensional fault structures from earthquake hypocenters. FaultNet uses two PointNet++-based models followed by agglomerative clustering and fault surface reconstruction by radial basis function. The first model, denoising model, identifies fault-related earthquakes and removes background seismicity. The second model, feature learning model, maps the remaining earthquakes into an embedding space in which earthquakes associated with the same fault have similar representations. Pairwise similarities estimated from overlapping spatial windows are combined into a global distance matrix and used for clustering. The resulting earthquake clusters can then be reconstructed as continuous three-dimensional fault surfaces using radial basis function (RBF) interpolation. ## Files and directories - `apply_FaultNet.ipynb`     Main notebook demonstrating the complete FaultNet inference workflow, including:   1. loading the trained models;   2. loading and visualizing an earthquake catalog;   3. selecting a sliding-window size;   4. identifying fault-related earthquakes;   5. learning feature embedding and agglomerative clustering;   6. reconstructing fault surfaces using RBF interpolation; and   7. evaluating and visualizing the reconstructed surfaces. - `example_catalog.npy`   Example earthquake catalog used in the notebook. The array has shape `(N, 5)`, with columns:   `x, y, z, horizontal_location_error, vertical_location_error`.   Spatial coordinates and location uncertainties should use consistent distance units (km in the provided example).   Users can replace it with another earthquake catalog following the same format. Coordinates and uncertainties should be expressed in a consistent Cartesian coordinate system and distance unit. - `example_prediction.npy`     Example FaultNet clustering output corresponding to `example_catalog.npy`. It contains one integer label per earthquake. A label of `-1` denotes background seismicity or clusters excluded by the minimum-size criterion (50 events); non-negative integers identify reconstructed fault clusters. - `model_I_denoising/`     Trained denoising model for distinguishing fault-related earthquakes from background seismicity. The trained weights used by the notebook are stored in `checkpoints/best_model.pth`. - `model_II_feature_learning/`     Trained feature learning model for generating 8-dimensional embedding representations of fault-related earthquakes. The trained weights used by the notebook are stored in `checkpoints/best_model.pth`. - `Pointnet_Pointnet2_pytorchmaster/`     PointNet++ implementation and supporting source code used by the FaultNet models. This directory is based on a PyTorch implementation of PointNet/PointNet++ and retains its associated license information. - `requirements.txt`     Python packages required by the main FaultNet notebook. ## Installation Python 3 is required. To install the main dependencies, run: ```bash pip install -r requirements.txt ``` The supplied notebook loads the trained neural networks on the CPU by default. PyTorch can be configured separately for CUDA-enabled GPU execution if desired.   ## Citation If you use FaultNet or the materials in this archive, please cite the associated FaultNet publication and this Zenodo record. .. 10.5281/zenodo.22837108 ## Acknowledgments This work was supported by the U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Science, Basic Energy Sciences (Award No. DE-SC0026319). ## License Please refer to the license information distributed with the relevant source-code components. Before public release, add the license selected for the FaultNet-specific code and trained models to the top-level archive.
items.title: FaultNet: Inferring Complex Fault Structures from Earthquake Hypocenter Distributions

items.summary: Metrics Added MixtureMetric and MixtureComponent , which express a weighted linear combination of BaseMetric instances. This is exact, by linearity of expectation, and is how empcs_score now expresses a distribution that mixes a point mass with a continuous piece — something a single Metric cannot express, since SymPy cannot symbolically integrate over such a distribution. Added BaseMetric , the abstraction every loss parameter throughout the package now accepts. Metric and MixtureMetric both implement it, so either can be passed interchangeably as a model's training objective. Added the LogCost strategy for building custom expected log cost (weighted cross-entropy) metrics. expected_log_cost_loss is now built from it. Metrics built with the Cost and Savings strategies now accept stochastic ( sympy.stats ) cost parameters, reducing them to their mean. Previously this raised NotImplementedError: Random variables are not supported for the savings metric. at Metric construction time. Added constrain and constrain , which declare the values a cost-matrix parameter is allowed to take. A parameter can be given inclusive lower / upper bounds, or a callable can express a condition spanning several parameters at once ( constrain(lambda p: p['clv'] > p['incentive_cost'], message=...) ). Added Profit , MinCost and EmpiricalMinCost , the sign-flipped siblings of Cost , MaxProfit and EmpiricalMaxProfit . Each computes the same quantity as its partner and reports it with the opposite sign, so a cost matrix can be read as costs to minimize or as profits to maximize. The choice is presentational: the optimal threshold and rate are unchanged, and models fit identically on either member of a pair. Added EmpiricalMaxProfit and AUEPC strategies for building custom metrics that compute the empirical (convex-hull-based) maximum profit and the area under the empirical profit curve, respectively. Metric now warns ( UserWarning ) at construction when the cost matrix has no terms, or its terms cancel to exactly zero — such a metric always evaluates to 0.0 regardless of its parameters. Metric now warns when called with a parameter its cost matrix does not use, instead of silently ignoring it — catching a typo'd keyword argument. sample_weight and strategy-specific extras (e.g. Savings ' baseline ) are exempt. Multi-letter symbols now render upright in the LaTeX representations of CostMatrix and Metric , so a product such as clv * r reads as two variables rather than as one named clvr . Greek names such as gamma are unaffected. MaxProfit with integration_method='auto' now uses quasi-Monte Carlo for any number of stochastic variables whose distributions can be sampled, rather than only above two. Two stochastic variables used to go to nested quadrature. Pass random_state for a result reproducible across Metric instances; repeated calls on one instance were already identical. Deterministic MaxProfit metrics (a profit function polynomial in the stochastic variable) no longer compute the ROC convex hull, and evaluate the profit function vectorized over all operating points instead of in a Python loop. Quasi-Monte Carlo integration now covers eleven more distributions: BoundedPareto , Dagum , ExponentialPower (not published in SymPy's own documentation, so no link is possible), Frechet , Gompertz , LogLogistic , RaisedCosine , Rayleigh , Reciprocal , Weibull and WignerSemicircle . These previously fell through to plain Monte Carlo, which is around a thousand times less accurate for the same sampling budget. optimal_rate and optimal_threshold now always compute the exact EMP when one stochastic variable is present. MaxProfit accepts profit functions of any shape in the stochastic variable. Previously a cost matrix using exp , log or a square root raised PolynomialError from inside SymPy when the Metric was constructed. check_input has been removed from every prebuilt metric that is now a Metric / MixtureMetric instance ( empc_score , mpc_score , empb_score

items.summary: The rise of generative AI has enabled the production of high-fidelity synthetic tabular data across fields such as healthcare, finance, and public policy, raising growing concerns about data provenance and misuse. Watermarking offers a promising solution to address these concerns by ensuring the traceability of synthetic data, but existing methods face many limitations: they are computationally expensive due to reliance on the inverse process of large diffusion models, struggle with mixed discrete-continuous data, or lack robustness to common post-processing attacks. To address these limitations, we propose TAB-DRW, an efficient and robust post-editing watermarking scheme for synthetic tabular data. TAB-DRW embeds watermark signals in the frequency domain: it normalizes heterogeneous features via the Yeo-Johnson transformation and standardization, applies the discrete Fourier transform (DFT), and adjusts the imaginary parts of adaptively selected entries according to precomputed pseudorandom bits. To further enhance robustness and efficiency, we introduce a novel rank-based pseudorandom bit generation method that enables row-wise retrieval without incurring storage overhead. Experiments on five benchmark tabular datasets show that TAB-DRW achieves strong detectability and robustness against post-processing and adaptive attacks, while preserving high data fidelity and fully supporting mixed-type features.
items.title: Robust Spectral Watermark for Synthetic Tabular Data

items.summary: Version 1.1 (2026-09-19). Version 1.0 stated that the English rebuild could not be compared against the published English store, because the cleaning pass behind that store no longer exists as a script. That was wrong: the missing script only prevents reproducing the Japanese/Chinese method, while the old English store and its index were on disk throughout. The comparison is now made, with the control questions generated from the old store's own chunk text — exactly what the old index encoded — over 400 articles sampled by uniform stride from the both-store intersection. Whole corpus, nprobe 128: the old store returns recall@1 19.5, recall@5 33.5, MRR 25.1; v11b returns 39.2, 59.5 and 47.9, a gain of +22.8 MRR while searching a corpus 2.9 times larger. Section 8.4 is new and records how four passes of review let an untested caveat stand. The results of version 1.0 are unchanged. We re-read three Wikipedia retrieval indexes we had published ourselves and had been using in production — English, Japanese and Chinese, FAISS over intfloat/multilingual-e5-large — and found three defects, none of which had ever produced an error message. Chunks were cut by character count in front of a token window, so 13.7 % of the published Japanese chunks and 18.5 % of the Chinese ones ran past the encoder's 512-token limit and lost 21.7 % and 27.0 % of their tokens at embed time. The Kiwix licence footer, 184 characters of English legal text, sat inside 97.1 % of the published Japanese chunks and 92.9 % of the Chinese ones. The index type, IndexIVFPQ(m=64) , returned 45.4–47.1 % of the exact top-10 and cost 7.8 MRR in Japanese and 10.7 in English against exact search. Rebuilding the whole pipeline moved retrieval against the previously published artifact from 26.6 to 43.3 MRR in Japanese and 26.2 to 47.5 in Chinese, on a control question set generated from the old extractor's own output. The components are not separated, and the rebuild is not uniformly better: indexed-article coverage falls in two of three languages. Two results may generalise. Our own first benchmark ranked the defective extractor higher , because it queried by article title, a field the index also stores. And clipping the scalar quantiser's range to the 0.1–99.9 percentile of the residuals rather than their min/max raises top-10 agreement with exact search from 81.6 % to 85.2 % at the same 4 bits per dimension; the first attempt computed the quantiles on raw vectors and made the index substantially worse, because an IVF index encodes residuals. Three rounds of adversarial review are reported at equal prominence with the results. Round one rejected the first rebuild. Round two found sixteen unsupported statements in the draft. Round three found a defect in the release that the first two had both passed — the acceptance script had not been re-run on two of the three shipped indexes after they were re-encoded — and three measurements that round two had itself introduced while correcting other numbers. Scope. This reports what happened to three specific artifacts. It does not claim these defects are common elsewhere. The retrieval numbers come from synthetic questions generated by one local model with no human relevance judgements and no answerability check; the reconstructed standard error of one MRR figure is 2.2–2.9 points. Index-type comparisons were run on pools of 150,000–206,000 vectors, not at the shipped scale of 3–15.6 million. Nothing here is peer reviewed, certified, or independently replicated; every reviewer was a model instance commissioned by the author. AI co-observer disclosure. The forensic measurements, the rebuild, the three review rounds and the drafting were carried out with Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic) as a working instrument under human direction. The registered author is the human author alone.
items.title: What a Retrieval Index Loses Before Anyone Notices: Three Silent Defects in Three Published Wikipedia Embedding Indexes

items.summary: Revision of the dataset prepared during peer review of the accompanying data descriptor at IEEE Data Descriptions . The 94 satellite–in-situ pairs and their concentration values are unchanged; what changes is how records are identified in time, what per-reservoir metadata is provided, and what guidance ships with the raw processor columns. Breaking change samples.csv no longer has a Date column. It is replaced by Campaign , with the values Summer YYYY and Autumn YYYY . The monitoring network samples these reservoirs twice a year, in June and in November, and the campaign label is what the compiled matchup table retains; the literal dates in v1.0.0 were a downstream conversion and should not be read as acquisition timestamps. Code written against v1.0.0 must be updated. Per-record acquisition timestamps were not retained when the table was compiled, so the individual in-situ/satellite temporal offsets cannot be recovered from these files. What is documented is the characterisation reported with the original processing (Cuartero et al., 2023): all 94 images fall inside the ±48 h selection window and 26% were acquired on the same day as the in-situ sample. Records cannot be filtered by temporal offset; studies for which simultaneity is critical should treat the whole collection as subject to an offset of up to two days. Added metadata.csv gains two morphometric descriptors per reservoir (15 → 17 columns): Eq. width (pix) , the equivalent width √A in 10 m pixels, and Window fraction (%) , the share of the water surface covered by a single 7×7 extraction window. Across the network the window fraction ranges from 0.26% to 49%. Users are advised to discard or treat separately any reservoir above about 25%. baseline_correction.py , a self-contained script (NumPy and pandas only) that fits a log–log correction log10(Chl) = a·log10(P) + b for each processor, plus a joint form over the three co-registered retrievals, and evaluates it under leave-one-reservoir-out cross-validation. Out-of-sample, it brings C2X from 639% to 39% MAPD and C2XC from 2181% to 43%; the joint form reaches 18%. It is a starting point and a sanity check, not a recommended retrieval, and its coefficients should not be transferred to other networks without refitting. Changed README updated for the new columns and the script, with a provenance note on time and a note on modelling with unevenly sampled reservoirs (Gini 0.32; effective number of equally weighted reservoirs 21.9 of 32). Use the reservoir, not the record, as the unit of resampling. The dataset is now named C2NEx-22, and the accompanying descriptor is identified as submitted to IEEE Data Descriptions .
items.title: C2NEx-22: A Paired Satellite–in-situ Chlorophyll-a in Extremadura, Spain for 32 Reservoirs Dataset

items.summary: This record contains the complete R and Python code and supporting documentation for the independent sensitivity reanalysis associated with the manuscript “Swab-based stool collection largely preserves gut microbiome structure with small device-dependent effects: an intra-individual evaluation of sampling devices and processing conditions.” The archive includes scripts to reconstruct and validate anonymous sample metadata from the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) run report and FASTQ filenames; perform preliminary read-quality and paired-read overlap assessments; process forward (R1) and reverse (R2) reads separately using DADA2; infer ASVs; assign taxonomy using the SILVA SSU NR99 release 138.2 training set; construct phylogenetic trees; evaluate sequencing-depth dependence; calculate standardized alpha- and beta-diversity metrics, including Faith’s phylogenetic diversity, weighted UniFrac, and Bray–Curtis dissimilarity; compare the R1 and R2 results; assess sensitivity to rarefaction depth and unusually long terminal branches; and generate the corresponding tables and figures. The archive also contains a complete execution guide, software dependencies and versions, random seeds, original R session information, reference-database details, and file-integrity checksums. Sample metadata and analytical outputs are generated locally by the documented workflow and are not distributed as precomputed files. Raw paired-end sequencing data are publicly available from the European Nucleotide Archive under accession PRJEB107991. The DADA2-formatted SILVA 138.2 taxonomic training set is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14169026 . The independent ASV analyses complement, but do not reproduce or replace, the proprietary MicrobAT® workflow used for the primary OTU-based analysis. MicrobAT® algorithms, OTU-assignment parameters, and the release of its embedded reference database were not disclosed by the software provider. Accordingly, this archive supports reproducibility of the independent R1/R2 ASV sensitivity analyses and downstream analyses of the published MicrobAT® outputs, but not reconstruction of the proprietary MicrobAT®-generated OTU and taxonomic profiles. This version supersedes the earlier R-only archive by adding the Python utilities, complete operational documentation, software-environment records, random seeds, integrity checks, and portable figure-generation scripts.
items.title: Reproducibility code for: Swab-based stool collection largely preserves gut microbiome structure with small device-dependent effects

items.summary: Ground deformation is the earliest measurable warning of a tailings-dam or pit-wall failure, and satellite interferometric synthetic-aperture radar (InSAR) can measure it at the millimetre scale over a whole facility. This report describes TailWatch, an interactive, reproducible studio that carries a deformation field from InSAR displacement to a failure forecast, and measures the accuracy of each stage. Two data lanes feed it: a high-fidelity synthetic Sentinel-1 forward simulation (von-Karman atmospheric phase screen, decorrelation, digital-elevation-model error and orbital ramps) over five deformation regimes, and one real case, the Campi Flegrei caldera from the open COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1 archive. A two-geometry Up/East decomposition resolves the synthetic line-of-sight field; a learned tier flags anomalies and classifies deformation type; and a classical inverse-velocity model forecasts the time of failure. All accuracies are measured on synthetic data. On held-out synthetic scenes the anomaly detectors are strong (velocity-based area-under-curve 0.968, autoencoder 0.898), and while the six-class deformation-type classifier is only moderate overall (macro-F1 0.556), it recovers the one class that matters for early warning, accelerating, at 0.99 recall. On 40 synthetic accelerating trajectories the inverse-velocity forecast detects every failure (100%) with a median failure-time error of 5.7%, tightening from about 14% far ahead to 2% close to failure, the behaviour a warning system needs, and it raises no false alarm on 60 non-accelerating synthetic controls. The Campi Flegrei series (2016-2018) contains no failure event, so no failure-time error can be measured on it; the studio computes its line-of-sight velocity, coherence and cumulative displacement, and runs the synthetic-trained detectors on it without ground truth. TailWatch is a didactic and decision-support instrument, not a certified safety system, and the small-baseline network inversion is not implemented. items.summary: Handwritten archival tables contain rich historical information, yet transforming them into structured representations, such as Knowledge Graphs, requires integrating table structure recognition, handwriting recognition, and semantic interpretation - a complex multimodal process. End-to-end AI implementations can obscure these steps, resulting in opaque algorithmic operations that hinder human oversight, critical assessment, and trust. To address this, we present a modular, provenance-aware pipeline to convert handwritten tabular images into KGs supporting human-AI collaboration. The pipeline decomposes the workflow into three stages - table reconstruction, information extraction, and KG construction - while exposing intermediate representations for inspection, evaluation, and correction. A key contribution of our approach is the systematic integration of data provenance at every stage, ensuring that all extracted entities and literals remain traceable to their visual and textual origins. The proposed pipeline is demonstrated through a number of experiments on real-world archival material concerning military careers. The results across three different table reconstruction variants highlight the importance of modularisation. By coupling modularity with data provenance, our work advances transparent and collaboratively controllable image-to-KG pipelines for complex historical data.
items.title: From Historical Tabular Image to Knowledge Graphs: A Provenance-Aware Modular Pipeline

items.summary: # FaultNet This archive contains the trained models, example earthquake catalog, and Jupyter notebook used to apply **FaultNet**, a deep-learning framework for reconstructing three-dimensional fault structures from earthquake hypocenters. FaultNet uses two PointNet++-based models followed by agglomerative clustering and fault surface reconstruction by radial basis function. The first model, denoising model, identifies fault-related earthquakes and removes background seismicity. The second model, feature learning model, maps the remaining earthquakes into an embedding space in which earthquakes associated with the same fault have similar representations. Pairwise similarities estimated from overlapping spatial windows are combined into a global distance matrix and used for clustering. The resulting earthquake clusters can then be reconstructed as continuous three-dimensional fault surfaces using radial basis function (RBF) interpolation. ## Files and directories - `apply_FaultNet.ipynb`     Main notebook demonstrating the complete FaultNet inference workflow, including:   1. loading the trained models;   2. loading and visualizing an earthquake catalog;   3. selecting a sliding-window size;   4. identifying fault-related earthquakes;   5. learning feature embedding and agglomerative clustering;   6. reconstructing fault surfaces using RBF interpolation; and   7. evaluating and visualizing the reconstructed surfaces. - `example_catalog.npy`   Example earthquake catalog used in the notebook. The array has shape `(N, 5)`, with columns:   `x, y, z, horizontal_location_error, vertical_location_error`.   Spatial coordinates and location uncertainties should use consistent distance units (km in the provided example).   Users can replace it with another earthquake catalog following the same format. Coordinates and uncertainties should be expressed in a consistent Cartesian coordinate system and distance unit. - `example_prediction.npy`     Example FaultNet clustering output corresponding to `example_catalog.npy`. It contains one integer label per earthquake. A label of `-1` denotes background seismicity or clusters excluded by the minimum-size criterion (50 events); non-negative integers identify reconstructed fault clusters. - `model_I_denoising/`     Trained denoising model for distinguishing fault-related earthquakes from background seismicity. The trained weights used by the notebook are stored in `checkpoints/best_model.pth`. - `model_II_feature_learning/`     Trained feature learning model for generating 8-dimensional embedding representations of fault-related earthquakes. The trained weights used by the notebook are stored in `checkpoints/best_model.pth`. - `Pointnet_Pointnet2_pytorchmaster/`     PointNet++ implementation and supporting source code used by the FaultNet models. This directory is based on a PyTorch implementation of PointNet/PointNet++ and retains its associated license information. - `requirements.txt`     Python packages required by the main FaultNet notebook. ## Installation Python 3 is required. To install the main dependencies, run: ```bash pip install -r requirements.txt ``` The supplied notebook loads the trained neural networks on the CPU by default. PyTorch can be configured separately for CUDA-enabled GPU execution if desired.   ## Citation If you use FaultNet or the materials in this archive, please cite the associated FaultNet publication and this Zenodo record. .. 10.5281/zenodo.22837108 ## Acknowledgments This work was supported by the U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Science, Basic Energy Sciences (Award No. DE-SC0026319). ## License Please refer to the license information distributed with the relevant source-code components. Before public release, add the license selected for the FaultNet-specific code and trained models to the top-level archive.

items.summary: State observation over the Hamilton division algebra is formulated as a structured realization problem for quaternionic multi-input multi-output systems. A left-intertwiner equation unifies companion assignment, row-oriented robust pole assignment, and coupled target realization with explicit noncommutative product order. A unitary measured-subspace decomposition yields a derivative-free observer with n-r dynamic quaternion states, where r = rank C, and reduces observability and detectability to a smaller pair. This order is minimal within the stated quaternion-linear full-state observer class. For full-order observers, structured H2 Lyapunov equations and an exact fixed-target gradient allow noise attenuation without moving the spectrum. For minimum-order observers, the reconstruction exposes the direct noise term and its interaction with pole-invariant injection freedom. Discrete-time formulas include the finite contribution of direct feedthrough, and correlated redundant outputs are characterized as noise references. Reproducible studies verify the gradients, compare quaternion, structured-complex, and real representations, expose the noise-cost nonuniqueness of maximum-volume designs, and test coupled repeated-class targets and a multi-output minimum-order observer.
items.title: Full- and Minimum-Order Quaternionic MIMO Observers: Spectral Assignment and Noise Geometry

items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed across diverse applications, raising critical questions for governance, accountability, and data provenance. Understanding which training data most influenced a model's output remains a fundamental open problem. We address this challenge through training data attribution (TDA) for auto-regressive LLMs by expanding upon the inverse formulation: How would training data be affected if the model had seen the generated output during training? Our method perturbs the base model using bidirectional gradient optimization (gradient ascent and descent) on a generated text sample and measures the resulting change in loss across training samples. Our framework supports attribution at arbitrary data granularity, enabling both factual and stylistic attribution. We evaluate our method against baselines on pretrained models with known datasets, and show that it outperforms previous work on influence metrics, thereby enhancing model interpretability, an essential requirement for accountable AI systems.
items.title: Data Attribution in Large Language Models via Bidirectional Gradient Optimization

items.summary: Ground deformation is the earliest measurable warning of a tailings-dam or pit-wall failure, and satellite interferometric synthetic-aperture radar (InSAR) can measure it at the millimetre scale over a whole facility. This report describes TailWatch, an interactive, reproducible studio that carries a deformation field from InSAR displacement to a failure forecast, and measures the accuracy of each stage. Two data lanes feed it: a high-fidelity synthetic Sentinel-1 forward simulation (von-Karman atmospheric phase screen, decorrelation, digital-elevation-model error and orbital ramps) over five deformation regimes, and one real case, the Campi Flegrei caldera from the open COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1 archive. A two-geometry Up/East decomposition resolves the synthetic line-of-sight field; a learned tier flags anomalies and classifies deformation type; and a classical inverse-velocity model forecasts the time of failure. All accuracies are measured on synthetic data. On held-out synthetic scenes the anomaly detectors are strong (velocity-based area-under-curve 0.968, autoencoder 0.898), and while the six-class deformation-type classifier is only moderate overall (macro-F1 0.556), it recovers the one class that matters for early warning, accelerating, at 0.99 recall. On 40 synthetic accelerating trajectories the inverse-velocity forecast detects every failure (100%) with a median failure-time error of 5.7%, tightening from about 14% far ahead to 2% close to failure, the behaviour a warning system needs, and it raises no false alarm on 60 non-accelerating synthetic controls. The Campi Flegrei series (2016-2018) contains no failure event, so no failure-time error can be measured on it; the studio computes its line-of-sight velocity, coherence and cumulative displacement, and runs the synthetic-trained detectors on it without ground truth. TailWatch is a didactic and decision-support instrument, not a certified safety system, and the small-baseline network inversion is not implemented. Every number and figure can be regenerated from the released artifacts. Interactive studio and reproducible pipeline (MIT): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_TailWatch . items.summary: This dataset contains the complete computational records from two 500-sequence demonstration runs performed with ENZTRA (Enzyme Redesign and Triage Automation), a reproducible and resumable workflow for reference-guided enzyme redesign. ENZTRA integrates reference preparation, RFdiffusion2 backbone generation, LigandMPNN sequence design, DLKcat and CatPred kinetic prediction, strict kinetic selection, Boltz-2 structural assessment, quality control, provenance tracking, and publication-oriented reporting. Both demonstrations used an active Escherichia coli phytase derived from PDB 1DKP and myo-inositol hexakisphosphate (IHP; phytate) as the reference enzyme-substrate system. Each run generated 50 RFdiffusion2 backbones and 10 LigandMPNN sequences per backbone, yielding 500 candidate sequences. The deposit contains two project archives: release-500: A short-scaffold demonstration using a requested design-length range of 150-180 residues. Fourteen of the 500 candidates satisfied the strict kinetic-selection criterion and proceeded to Boltz-2 structural assessment. The remaining 486 candidates were rejected, and no data-quality failures were detected. release-500b: A full-length comparison using a requested scaffold length of 410 residues, matching the reference sequence length. All 500 candidates passed the specified data-quality checks, but none satisfied the strict kinetic-selection criterion because their predicted turnover numbers were below the reference prediction. Consequently, no candidate proceeded to Boltz-2 assessment. The ENZTRA strict kinetic gate requires both a predicted turnover number ( k cat) above the corresponding reference value and a predicted Michaelis constant ( K m) below the reference value. Passing data-quality checks is therefore distinct from passing kinetic selection. The archives include validated biological inputs, design requests, RFdiffusion2 specifications and execution records, generated backbones, TRB and functional-site mappings, LigandMPNN outputs, consolidated sequence files, DLKcat and CatPred inputs and predictions, kinetic and selection tables, Boltz-2 inputs and outputs where applicable, quality-control tables, publication figures, workflow-state records, qualification reports, and reproducibility manifests. These results are computational predictions intended to demonstrate workflow execution, traceability, recovery, candidate selection, and reporting. They do not establish catalytic activity, structural correctness, expression, stability, or experimental improvement. All prioritized candidates require appropriate experimental validation. ENZTRA source code, installation instructions, and a step-by-step reproduction tutorial are available at: https://github.com/Olanrewaju-Durojaye/ENZTRA

items.summary: We present SemRepo, an RDF knowledge graph comprising over 81 million triples describing nearly 200,000 GitHub repositories associated with scientific research. SemRepo captures repository-level metadata, such as contributors, issues, and programming languages, and interlinks this information with external scholarly knowledge graphs. In particular, repository authors are linked to their profiles in SemOpenAlex, repositories are connected to scholarly publications in LPWC, and research artifacts, such as datasets and experiments, are linked via MLSea-KG. This integration enables queries that span publications and their scholarly artifacts, which are typically fragmented across separate platforms. SemRepo supports analyses that are difficult to perform with existing resources in isolation, including provenance reconstruction across repositories and publications, as well as the systematic identification of risks to research reproducibility and software sustainability. By unifying research software with its scholarly context in a single graph, SemRepo provides an important infrastructure for large-scale analysis of software within the broader scientific research ecosystem.
items.title: SemRepo: A Knowledge Graph for Research Software and Its Scholarly Ecosystem

items.summary: Background. Frailty is often raised as a reason to withhold complete revascularization from older patients after myocardial infarction, although the FIRE trial found no interaction between frailty and the benefit of physiology-guided complete revascularization. Objective. To estimate the cost-effectiveness of physiology-guided complete versus culprit-lesion-only revascularization after successful culprit-lesion percutaneous coronary intervention in patients aged 75 years or older with myocardial infarction and multivessel disease, overall and across Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) strata, from the German statutory health insurance perspective. Methods. A three-year cohort model with quarterly cycles was anchored to the FIRE marginal outcomes (primary composite of death, myocardial infarction, stroke or ischaemia-driven revascularization 22.9% versus 29.8%; cardiovascular death or myocardial infarction 12.8% versus 18.2%; heart-failure hospitalisation 14.3% versus 19.7%). Risks in CFS 1-3, 4 and 5-9 were obtained by external calibration that preserved these trial marginals, with a relative treatment effect common to all strata. Costs used 2026 German diagnosis-related-group tariffs. Every input was classified by provenance, and uncertainty was assessed with 20,000 probabilistic draws, one-way and scenario analyses, and break-even analysis. Results. Complete revascularization cost EUR 757 more per patient and yielded 0.056 additional quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs), an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of EUR 13,601 per QALY. Ratios were EUR 20,541 per QALY in CFS 1-3, EUR 8,640 in CFS 4 and EUR 8,662 in CFS 5-9. The probability of cost-effectiveness at EUR 30,000 per QALY was 92.5% overall and 78.6%, 96.5% and 97.7% across strata. At that value, the minimum three-year absolute reduction in the primary composite required for cost-effectiveness was 4.3 per 100 patients overall, against a modelled trial effect of 6.9. Staging the additional procedure as a separate admission was the most influential cost driver. Conclusions. Within three years, physiology-guided complete revascularization appears cost-effective at reference values of EUR 20,000 to EUR 50,000 per QALY, and estimated cost-effectiveness was not attenuated in the frailer strata. The stratum-specific estimates rest on external frailty calibration rather than on frailty-specific FIRE outcomes and are not evidence of effect modification.
items.title: Cost-Effectiveness of Physiology-Guided Complete Revascularization Across Frailty Strata in Older Patients with Myocardial Infarction: A German Analysis Informed by the FIRE Trial

items.summary: Ground deformation is the earliest measurable warning of a tailings-dam or pit-wall failure, and satellite interferometric synthetic-aperture radar (InSAR) can measure it at the millimetre scale over a whole facility. This report describes TailWatch, an interactive, reproducible studio that carries a deformation field from InSAR displacement to a failure forecast, and measures the accuracy of each stage. Two data lanes feed it: a high-fidelity synthetic Sentinel-1 forward simulation (von-Karman atmospheric phase screen, decorrelation, digital-elevation-model error and orbital ramps) over five deformation regimes, and one real case, the Campi Flegrei caldera from the open COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1 archive. A two-geometry Up/East decomposition resolves the synthetic line-of-sight field; a learned tier flags anomalies and classifies deformation type; and a classical inverse-velocity model forecasts the time of failure. All accuracies are measured on synthetic data. On held-out synthetic scenes the anomaly detectors are strong (velocity-based area-under-curve 0.968, autoencoder 0.898), and while the six-class deformation-type classifier is only moderate overall (macro-F1 0.556), it recovers the one class that matters for early warning, accelerating, at 0.99 recall. On 40 synthetic accelerating trajectories the inverse-velocity forecast detects every failure (100%) with a median failure-time error of 5.7%, tightening from about 14% far ahead to 2% close to failure, the behaviour a warning system needs, and it raises no false alarm on 60 non-accelerating synthetic controls. The Campi Flegrei series (2016-2018) contains no failure event, so no failure-time error can be measured on it; the studio computes its line-of-sight velocity, coherence and cumulative displacement, and runs the synthetic-trained detectors on it without ground truth. TailWatch is a didactic and decision-support instrument, not a certified safety system, and the small-baseline network inversion is not implemented. Every number and figure can be regenerated from the released artifacts. Interactive studio and reproducible pipeline (MIT): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CAOS_TailWatch . Interactive studio: https://tailwatch.fasl-work.com . Real-case data: COMET LiCSAR/LiCSBAS Sentinel-1, descending frame 124D_04854_171313 (2016-2018), redistributed under the Copernicus free-and-open licence with LiCSBAS attribution (Morishita et al. 2020); provenance in data/derived/tw-real-cf.provenance.json.
items.title: TailWatch: An InSAR Deformation-Monitoring and Inverse-Velocity Failure-Forecasting Studio, on Synthetic Sentinel-1 and Real Campi Flegrei

items.summary: This dataset contains the complete computational records from two 500-sequence demonstration runs performed with ENZTRA (Enzyme Redesign and Triage Automation), a reproducible and resumable workflow for reference-guided enzyme redesign. ENZTRA integrates reference preparation, RFdiffusion2 backbone generation, LigandMPNN sequence design, DLKcat and CatPred kinetic prediction, strict kinetic selection, Boltz-2 structural assessment, quality control, provenance tracking, and publication-oriented reporting. Both demonstrations used an active Escherichia coli phytase derived from PDB 1DKP and myo-inositol hexakisphosphate (IHP; phytate) as the reference enzyme-substrate system. Each run generated 50 RFdiffusion2 backbones and 10 LigandMPNN sequences per backbone, yielding 500 candidate sequences. The deposit contains two project archives: release-500: A short-scaffold demonstration using a requested design-length range of 150-180 residues. Fourteen of the 500 candidates satisfied the strict kinetic-selection criterion and proceeded to Boltz-2 structural assessment. The remaining 486 candidates were rejected, and no data-quality failures were detected. release-500b: A full-length comparison using a requested scaffold length of 410 residues, matching the reference sequence length. All 500 candidates passed the specified data-quality checks, but none satisfied the strict kinetic-selection criterion because their predicted turnover numbers were below the reference prediction. Consequently, no candidate proceeded to Boltz-2 assessment. The ENZTRA strict kinetic gate requires both a predicted turnover number ( k cat) above the corresponding reference value and a predicted Michaelis constant ( K m) below the reference value. Passing data-quality checks is therefore distinct from passing kinetic selection. The archives include validated biological inputs, design requests, RFdiffusion2 specifications and execution records, generated backbones, TRB and functional-site mappings, LigandMPNN outputs, consolidated sequence files, DLKcat and CatPred inputs and predictions, kinetic and selection tables, Boltz-2 inputs and outputs where applicable, quality-control tables, publication figures, workflow-state records, qualification reports, and reproducibility manifests. These results are computational predictions intended to demonstrate workflow execution, traceability, recovery, candidate selection, and reporting. They do not establish catalytic activity, structural correctness, expression, stability, or experimental improvement. All prioritized candidates require appropriate experimental validation. ENZTRA source code, installation instructions, and a step-by-step reproduction tutorial are available at: https://github.com/Olanrewaju-Durojaye/ENZTRA

items.summary: Hashing Is Not Retrieval is a prospectively frozen three-arm evaluation of context accumulation in small-model multi-agent code cartography. It compares three ways for an orchestrator to hand work to a worker: 1. FULL HISTORY — retransmit prior worker outputs. 2. OPAQUE REF — replace the previous output with an unretrievable SHA-256 digest. 3. RETRIEVED — resolve the digest through a tenant-scoped content-addressed store and inject the recovered bytes. All arms receive identical source-derived evidence. The apparatus measures the exact message content sent to workers and records token counts, model and provider identifiers, generation IDs, usage, cost, retries, and retrieval proofs. A five-task gate preceded a fixed 50-task controlled benchmark, followed by a separate state-required evaluation across 24 deterministic fixtures and a five-scale Medusa case study. Key result: in the controlled benchmark, RETRIEVED reduced paired peak context by 38.3% relative to FULL HISTORY. The state-required follow-up shows that opaque references fail when state must be recovered, while verified retrieval preserves substantially more structural information. This is bounded-context evidence for automatic orchestrator-resolved state passing inside a specific two-worker code-cartography harness — not a universal claim about autonomous memory, long-context capability, or reasoning quality. The release includes the corrected author-identified preprint, executable apparatus, frozen results, task fixtures, telemetry, and verification instructions. Version 1.0.2 supplies the curated, verifier-passing reproducibility archive. It supersedes the uncurated archive from version 1.0.1 and includes the exact pinned apparatus, state-required fixtures, frozen results, and archive verifier. items.summary: This repository contains the data, documentation, and replication materials associated with the data paper on the  Cartulario de Santo Toribio de Liébana . The dataset provides a structured reconstruction of the documentary collection edited by Luis Sánchez Belda and converts the information contained in the cartulary into machine-readable research data. It covers 566 documentary acts and includes linked information on 576 payment or counter-performance elements, 603 place names, and 1,348 identified persons , together with a concordance between documentary numbering systems. The package preserves the documentary structure of the source while providing standardized variables suitable for quantitative and computational historical research. Particular attention is given to economic transactions. Payments and other forms of material counter-performance are recorded at the individual-component level rather than collapsed into a single transaction value. The data also distinguish operative contractual provisions from penalty clauses and other formulaic diplomatic material. Contains the materials required to reproduce and audit the construction of the dataset, including the structured datasets, extraction and coding documentation, variable definitions, provenance information, validation materials, and the code used for data processing and quality-control procedures. The replication workflow documents the transformation from the published documentary source to the final structured tables. It records corrections and normalization decisions while maintaining traceability to the underlying documentary act. The package is therefore intended not only to reproduce the published dataset but also to make individual coding decisions auditable. The dataset is designed for reuse in research on medieval economic history, property transactions, monastic institutions, historical geography, social networks, and computational approaches to diplomatic sources.

items.summary: Derived tables and provenance registries supporting source-resolved mass absorption efficiency (MAE) estimates for wintertime brown carbon from residential solid-fuel and fossil-fuel combustion across European and Chinese sites. Contents: (i) source-resolved MAE estimates for the European station pairs and six Chinese cities with block-bootstrap percentile intervals and trustworthiness grading; (ii) station metadata and the field-level verification status of the Chinese records; (iii) per-dataset variable-group coverage tables and sensitivity analyses; (iv) the 84-field variable dictionary of the harmonized master table; (v) per-dataset provenance registries recording authoritative archives, citations and access routes, including a per-file DOI registry for the EBAS absorption compilation; (vi) the evidence tables underlying the Supporting Information (spectral benchmarks, coverage analyses, validation tables, perturbation domains, and the literature-coordinate conversion audit); (vii) an integrity baseline of file checksums for independent verification. Primary hourly records are not redistributed and are available from the original archives identified in the provenance registry or from the authors on request. The harmonized master table itself is not included. Earlier versions and superseded analyses are documented in the version history; the current release is the curated final set. v1.7.0 (2026-09-20) : third-round revision-companion update. Adds the pricing estimand registry (coal: Kraków 2018/19 pure-CCOA median 4.61 m² g⁻¹; biofuel: five-station winter-matched effective 3.84 m² g⁻¹), the source-omission benchmark with locked-λ bootstrap loss distributions, placebo arms and model-available bulk predictors, the unified canonical interval products and block-length sensitivities, the canonical-construction coverage harness, the conditional-ratio bootstrap draws, the locked SI table mirrors (SI_Table_S26–S31.csv), and the figure-generation and 370 nm conversion scripts. See README_v1.7.0_addendum.md inside the archive for the file-level inventory.

items.summary: Cyber threats directed against space systems (spanning orbital payloads, tracking and telemetry ground stations, downlinks, and upstream manufacturing supply chains) have evolved into acute operational hazards. Concurrently, national security and commercial defenders face an intelligence volume crisis where telemetry and vulnerability disclosures outpace human cognitive bandwidth. While autonomous multi-agent pipelines powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) offer scalable automation, they introduce severe epistemic liabilities: hallucination, source detachment, uncalibrated certainty, and susceptibility to indirect prompt injection. This paper presents Space-Cyber Brief Crew, a multi-agent cyber threat intelligence (CTI) architecture that automates space-domain intelligence synthesis under an explicit governance layer. Built on a decoupled CrewAI orchestration, the system routes structured reporting through a three-stage sequential pipeline (Collector, Analyst, Writer) governed by ten operational rules. Crucially, the architecture establishes a structural boundary between action capabilities and generative synthesis: downstream analysis agents operate in zero-tool sandboxes, restricting the execution attack surface by construction. We evaluate the framework against a tri-domain threat corpus spanning satellite imagery manipulation, ground industrial control systems (ICS), and global navigation satellite system (GNSS) spoofing. In our evaluation, the governed architecture eliminated identifier fabrication (from 23.3% to 0.0%), preserved 100% provenance retention, and neutralized indirect prompt injection attacks that succeeded in 80% of unconstrained baseline runs. Finally, we examine the institutional, regulatory, and oversight implications, establishing technical criteria for federal procurement and intelligence integration.

items.summary: Hashing Is Not Retrieval is a prospectively frozen three-arm evaluation of context accumulation in small-model multi-agent code cartography. It compares three ways for an orchestrator to hand work to a worker: 1. FULL HISTORY — retransmit prior worker outputs. 2. OPAQUE REF — replace the previous output with an unretrievable SHA-256 digest. 3. RETRIEVED — resolve the digest through a tenant-scoped content-addressed store and inject the recovered bytes. All arms receive identical source-derived evidence. The apparatus measures the exact message content sent to workers and records token counts, model and provider identifiers, generation IDs, usage, cost, retries, and retrieval proofs. A five-task gate preceded a fixed 50-task controlled benchmark, followed by a separate state-required evaluation across 24 deterministic fixtures and a five-scale Medusa case study. Key result: in the controlled benchmark, RETRIEVED reduced paired peak context by 38.3% relative to FULL HISTORY. The state-required follow-up shows that opaque references fail when state must be recovered, while verified retrieval preserves substantially more structural information. This is bounded-context evidence for automatic orchestrator-resolved state passing inside a specific two-worker code-cartography harness — not a universal claim about autonomous memory, long-context capability, or reasoning quality. The release includes the corrected author-identified preprint, executable apparatus, frozen results, task fixtures, telemetry, and verification instructions. Version 1.0.2 supplies the curated, verifier-passing reproducibility archive. It supersedes the uncurated archive from version 1.0.1 and includes the exact pinned apparatus, state-required fixtures, frozen results, and archive verifier. Submission status: This preprint was submitted to the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Long Context Foundation Models (LCFM). LCFM is a non-archival workshop; this Zenodo record is a public preprint and does not indicate acceptance or publication. items.summary: This deposit contains the analysis code, fitted parameters, output files, audit records, supplements, and citation list supporting the working paper "Power-Law Claims in Production and Supply Networks: What Survives a Uniform Certification Audit" (version 16, September 2026, posted on SSRN) by Bruce Rishel (Independent Scholar, ORCID 0009-0000-8324-4331) and Melissa Rishel (Independent Scholar, ORCID 0009-0001-4919-0728). Melissa Rishel contributed the independent validation of the statistical analysis and the mathematical derivations. The audit applies the Clauset-Shalizi-Newman 2009 maximum-likelihood estimation protocol with semi-parametric bootstrap goodness-of-fit testing and likelihood-ratio tests against alternative distributions, together with the Broido-Clauset 2019 five-category corpus classification, to a verified population of 20 published power-law claims in the supply chain operational literature. Three widely cited datasets are re-analyzed. The manuscript reports four distributions: Acemoglu et al. 2012's sectoral input-output out-degree (BEA 1997 Use Table), Liu, Shen, Tan 2021's international trade product networks in both the out-degree and in-degree directions (BACI HS92 Y2024 current release, 1,217 networks), and Axtell 2001's US firm-size distribution (SUSB 2017, n = 5,996,900 firms via the Virkar-Clauset 2014 binned-data MLE). The Acemoglu influence vector is analyzed separately and treated as exploratory, described under the version note below. The remaining 17 audit targets are characterized at methodology rigor level without independent data re-analysis. Every audit-target citation is verified against its publisher record for title, authors, DOI, and the cited claim text. Contents of the deposit: analysis/: Python implementation of the audit's re-analysis pipeline: BACI parsing and corpus fitting, BEA 1997 Use Table reconstruction, SUSB binned-data MLE via Virkar-Clauset 2014, Vuong likelihood-ratio tests, Broido-Clauset 2019 corpus classification, semi-parametric bootstrap goodness-of-fit, the exploratory influence-vector sensitivity engine, and cross-validation of the Acemoglu first-order out-degree re-analysis against the published Alstott et al. 2014 powerlaw Python library, where fitted exponents and Kolmogorov-Smirnov distances match to four decimal places. The influence-vector exponent reflects that library's default parameter-range cap at 3.0 and is treated as exploratory; the closed-form maximum-likelihood value on the same input lies above 3. outputs/: JSON output files containing per-target fitted parameters, x_min values, KS distances, bootstrap p-values, Vuong test statistics, and corpus aggregate statistics, plus the powerlaw-library cross-validation output and the exploratory influence-vector sensitivity results. audit_records/: per-target audit records for the three re-analyzed datasets (Acemoglu et al. 2012, Liu-Shen-Tan 2021, Axtell 2001), including methodology grade, data acquisition tier, sample sizes, fit details, and audit verdict. audit_targets/: structured audit-target list of all 20 verified entries with author, title, venue, year, DOI, verification status, data tier, methodology rigor level, and re-analysis results. verification_protocol.md: the citation-verification procedure used to assemble the audit population. references.md: the manuscript's numbered reference list. figures/: three figures from the manuscript, the BACI corpus alpha distributions, the Acemoglu d_i CCDF with fitted power law, and the SUSB firm-size CCDF with fitted power law. README.md: file inventory, dependency versions, reproducibility instructions, and citation guidance. CHANGELOG.md: version history of this deposit. LICENSE: MIT License (code), CC-BY 4.0 (documentation). Data sources used by the audit code are public and free: the BEA 1997 detailed Use Table (Bureau of Economic Analysis), the BACI HS92 Y2024 release (CEPII), and the SUSB 2017 US enterprise-size brackets (US Census Bureau).
